system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2159-04-23 16:15:00 to 2159-04-25 16:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, type II diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and heart failure was admitted for evaluation of a nonhealing foot ulcer following a prior toe amputation. He underwent a right lower extremity angiogram to assess blood flow, which showed arterial blockages but sufficient perfusion for healing. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout the admission. On postoperative day one, he developed hyperkalemia with a potassium rise from 5.5 to 6.5, prompting an urgent two-hour hemodialysis session with a low-potassium bath. His lisinopril was discontinued and amlodipine increased per nephrology guidance. He was discharged home on day two in stable condition with medication adjustments, wound care instructions, and follow-up arranged with vascular surgery.
problems: Ulcer of other part of foot
Amputation of limb(s) causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure

access.

for occlusion and thrombectomy.
 
COMPARISON:  U/S ___.

the fellow.
 
MEDICATIONS:  Fentanyl (25 mcg).  tPA was administered via the AngioJet device
for a total of 10 mg.  4000 units of heparin was administered systemically. 
Local anesthesia was provided with approximately 10 cc of 1% lidocaine.
 
FLUOROSCOPY:  38.4 minutes, 158 mGy

CONTRAST: 110 mL Optiray

PROCEDURE:  
1. RUE AV graft fistulogram.
2. Balloon angioplasty of the right brachiocephalic vein stenosis. 
3. Chemical and mechanical thrombolysis of thrombosed graft.
4. ___ balloon sweep of the arterial inflow.
5. Balloon angioplasty of the intragraft stenosis.
 
DESCRIPTION:  After written informed consent was obtained, the patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The
left upper extremity was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed per the ___ protocol.
 
Clinical examination demonstrated a firm , palpable but non-pulsatile graft in
the right upper arm.  Further evaluation by ultrasound demonstrated a
completely thrombosed graft with patent arterial inflow and venous outflow. 
Using ultrasound and fluoroscopy, the inflow and outflow levels were
identified and the skin was marked with an indelible marker. 
 
Antegrade access into the thrombosed graft (directed towards the venous
outflow) was obtained using a micropuncture system .  The micropuncture wire
was exchanged for a Glidewire and the micropuncture sheath upsized to a ___ Fr
___ tip sheath. The Glidewire was advanced into the outflow vein and with
the assistance of a Kumpe catheter, multiple attempts were made to gain
central access, but were unsuccessful. Digital subtraction venogram
demonstrated complete occlusion of the bracheocepalic-SVC confluence.  Using
the venogram for guidance, a Glidewire was eventually advanced across the
stenosis into IVC. The wire was then exchanged for a ___ wire with the
assistance of the Kumpe catheter. 

We then turned our attention to the retrograde access and used ultrasound
guidance and a micropuncture access system to advance a glide wire through
soft clot within the graft.  A 6 sheath was then advanced over the glide wire.
Care was taken not to advance the wire into the inflow artery prior to
chemical thrombolysis. At this time, balloon angioplasty of the central
stenosis was performed with a 6 mm balloon.

The AngioJet device was placed in thrombectomy mode and mechanical
thrombectomy was performed from the antegrade and retrograde approach and
repeated twice. Next, tPA was administered using the AngioJet pulse spray
device in the anterograde direction for a total of 6 mg beginning at the
proximal aspect of the stent.  Further tPA was administered for a total of 4
mg in a retrograde fashion from the arterial anastomosis back into the mid
graft.  The tPA was allowed to dwell for approximately 10 minutes. Mechanical
thrombectomy was repeated.  Balloon maceration was performed throughout the
graft using a 6 mm balloon.  The antegrade sheath was then connected to a side
arm heparinized saline flush. 
 
Next, our attention was turned to the arterial inflow.  A ___ balloon
pull-back sweep was performed to the tip of the retrograde sheath using a
___ embolectomy balloon. This resulted in improved flow and a faint thrill
in the graft. A Kumpe catheter was advanced over the glide wire allowing a
full angiographic run outlining the entire graft and the central veins
demonstrating residual outflow vein and central venous stenosis. Repeat
angioplasty of the central stenosis was performed with an 8 mm and 10 mm
balloon, sequentially. 
 
Repeat fistulagram demonstrated significant improvement with moderate residual
stenosis.  The sheaths were then removed and hemostasis was achieved with
pursestring sutures.  There was no immediate complications. A satisfactory
thrill was noted in the graft at the termination of the procedure.

The patient was transferred to dialysis.
 
FINDINGS:

1.  RUE graft thrombosis. Restoration of flow in the  graft following
mechanical and pharmacologic thrombectomy.

2.  Complete chronic occlusion of the left brachiocephalic vein with multiple
collaterals. Moderate residual stenosis following sequential balloon
angioplasty up to 10 mm.

IMPRESSION:
 
1.  Thrombectomy of right forearm AV graft using an AngioJet device and 10 mg
of TPA.
 
2.  ___ embolectomy of the arterial anastomosis.
 
3.  Balloon angioplasty of the brachiocephalic vein to 10 mm.
 
4.  Angioplasty of intragraft stenosis to 6 mm.
  
5.  Satisfactory restoration of flow was achieved with a palpable thrill on
examination. The patient should return for elective repeat balloon angioplasty
of the central stenosis in ___ weeks. This lesion may require stenting if it
re occludes in the short term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because your dialysis fistula wasn’t working today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at dialysis they said no blood was flowing. My right arm fistula—just stopped working. I didn’t feel any pain or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We checked with an ultrasound, and it shows the graft is completely clotted. That’s why the blood couldn’t flow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that dangerous? I’ve had this fistula less than a year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious because you need it for dialysis, but we can fix it. The interventional radiology team will do a procedure tomorrow to clear the clot and open up the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to go home after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how it goes. You’ll likely stay one night, maybe two. You’ll get dialysis here while we fix the fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My wife is here—she can help translate if I don’t understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ll make sure you both understand everything. For now, you need to stay NPO—nothing to eat or drink—after midnight in case of the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nothing to eat? Even water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No food or drink, not even water, after midnight. It’s for your safety during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure and labs—they looked okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Potassium is a bit high at 5.3, but not dangerous right now. Your kidney numbers are expected for someone on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had high potassium before—caused heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your history. We’ll be careful with your medications and make sure you get dialysis soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The radiology team is ready to do the procedure. They’ll use a special machine to open the clot in your fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll give you medicine to help you relax and numb the area. You might feel some pressure, but not sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And they’ll fix the whole thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll clear the clot and open up a narrowing in the vein. But they’re concerned it might narrow again, so you may need another procedure soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. They found a tight spot in the large vein near your chest. Even after opening it, it could close again. They’ll schedule a follow-up in the next two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the procedure. They successfully cleared the clot and opened the narrowed vein using balloons.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt some pressure, but okay. Is it fixed now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fistula is working again—there’s good blood flow and a strong thrill. But there’s still some narrowing, so you’ll need to go back for another check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call you with an appointment in the next two weeks. If it closes again, they might need to place a stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a full dialysis session this afternoon. After that, you can go back to your normal M-W-F schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs after the procedure look stable. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but expected. Potassium is now 5.8—still okay since you’ll dialyze soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? I’m diabetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was high at 362, but that’s common in the hospital. We kept your insulin lower since you were NPO. At home, go back to your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I check it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, check your blood sugar regularly. If it’s below 100, reduce your glargine to 7 units and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on all your usual medications—amlodipine, aspirin, sevelamer, pravastatin, and the rest. We restarted your gabapentin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re doing well. Your fistula has a strong thrill, and you’re stable. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. When will I hear about the follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology team will call you within the next two weeks to schedule the next procedure. Keep checking your fistula daily for a thrill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And dialysis on Monday as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume your normal dialysis schedule. And don’t forget to monitor your blood sugar and take all your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, type II diabetes, and heart failure was admitted due to a thrombosed right brachiobasilic fistula. He underwent a successful thrombectomy and balloon angioplasty to restore blood flow, with residual stenosis noted in the central vein. He received a dialysis session during admission and was stabilized on his home medications. The interventional radiology team expressed concern about recurrent stenosis and will schedule a follow-up procedure within two weeks. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to resume dialysis, monitor blood glucose, and watch for fistula function.
